ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Thyroid cancer is a malignant tumor of thyroid follicular cells (papillary, follicular) or parafollicular C‑cells (medullary). Diagnosis relies on ultrasound, fine‑needle aspiration, and histology, and management combines surgery, radioactive iodine, and lifelong monitoring.

sections.p: Thyroid cancer is a neoplasm arising from thyroid tissue, most commonly papillary (80%) followed by follicular, medullary, and anaplastic types. Diagnosis requires suspicious nodule on ultrasound, cytology by fine‑needle aspiration (FNA), and confirmation by histopathology after surgery.
b: Ultrasound features: hypoechoic, microcalcifications, irregular margins, taller‑than‑wide shape.
FNA cytology: Bethesda system; categories V–VI indicate malignancy.

t.b: Does the nodule have high‑risk sonographic features? Positive findings raise suspicion and prompt FNA.
What is the cytology classification? Bethesda V or VI confirms cancer; lower categories may need repeat FNA or observation.
Is medullary thyroid carcinoma suspected (family history, MEN2)? Elevated calcitonin supports MTC diagnosis.
Is there a hereditary medullary carcinoma? Positive RET mutation guides prophylactic thyroidectomy.

sections.p: Staging uses the AJCC/TNM system: tumor size (T), nodal involvement (N), distant metastasis (M), and patient age (<45 vs ≥45). Stage I–II are low risk; Stage III–IV carry higher mortality, especially anaplastic carcinoma.
b: T1 ≤2 cm, T2 >2 cm ≤4 cm, T3 >4 cm or minimal extrathyroidal extension, T4 gross invasion.
N0–N1 based on central and lateral neck nodes.
M0 vs M1 (lung, bone).

sections.p: Most thyroid cancers are sporadic; risk factors include radiation exposure, family history, and certain genetic syndromes.
b: Prior head/neck radiation (especially in childhood).
Familial non‑medullary thyroid cancer (e.g., PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome).
RET proto‑oncogene mutation – medullary thyroid carcinoma.
Iodine deficiency (follicular carcinoma) – relevant in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Often a painless, slowly enlarging neck nodule; many are incidentally found on imaging. Symptoms of compression (dysphagia, hoarseness) suggest advanced disease.
b: Asymptomatic thyroid nodule on exam or ultrasound.
Occasional cervical lymphadenopathy.
Rarely, hyperthyroidism in toxic nodules.

sections.p: Beyond imaging and cytology, labs and functional studies guide treatment and identify hereditary forms.
b: Thyroglobulin (post‑thyroidectomy) monitors residual disease.
Serum calcium and PTH after surgery to detect hypoparathyroidism.

t.b: Is there residual or recurrent disease after total thyroidectomy? Rising levels indicate recurrence.
Does the tumor take up iodine? Positive uptake guides radioactive iodine therapy; negative suggests non‑iodine‑avid disease.
Is there extrathyroidal extension or distant metastasis? Imaging defines surgical planning and staging.

sections.p: Rapid growth, airway compromise, or distant metastasis require urgent intervention. Complications of treatment include hypocalcemia, recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, and secondary malignancies from radioactive iodine.
b: Stridor or severe dysphagia → airway obstruction.
Hypercalcemia in medullary carcinoma (calcitonin‑producing).
Secondary malignancies after high‑dose I‑131.

sections.p: Surgery is first‑line; total thyroidectomy for tumors >1 cm or with nodal disease. Radioactive iodine ablation is used for iodine‑avid differentiated cancers. Lifelong levothyroxine suppresses TSH. Medullary carcinoma requires total thyroidectomy plus central neck dissection; no I‑131 benefit.
b: Total or near‑total thyroidectomy – removes primary tumor and allows radioactive iodine.
Radioactive iodine (I‑131) – destroys residual thyroid tissue; chosen for iodine‑avid differentiated cancers.
Levothyroxine – suppresses TSH, reducing stimulation of residual cancer cells.
Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g., vandetanib) – for progressive medullary carcinoma when surgery not curative.

sections.p: After surgery, monitor thyroglobulin, neck ultrasound, and TSH levels every 6–12 months. Patients with familial syndromes need genetic counseling and screening of relatives.
b: Annual neck ultrasound for the first 5 years.
Serum thyroglobulin every 6 months (post‑thyroidectomy).
Screen at-risk family members with ultrasound and RET testing.

sections.p: Benign thyroid nodules, thyroiditis, and metastatic neck lymph nodes can mimic cancer on imaging.
b: Multinodular goiter – multiple benign nodules, usually non‑suspicious on ultrasound.
Hashimoto thyroiditis – hypoechoic heterogeneous gland, may have false‑positive FNA.
Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma to cervical nodes – can appear as suspicious lymphadenopathy.

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely reassuring; clinicians must interpret them in context.
b: Negative FNA in a large, suspicious nodule – sampling error; repeat FNA or core biopsy may be needed.
Low thyroglobulin after total thyroidectomy without adequate TSH stimulation – may miss residual disease.
Normal calcitonin in early medullary carcinoma – can be within reference range; repeat testing if suspicion persists.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden neck swelling with difficulty breathing or swallowing

faq.a: No; differentiated thyroid cancers have >95 % 10‑year survival when treated early.

faq.q: Why is radioactive iodine not used for medullary carcinoma?
faq.a: Medullary cells do not take up iodine, so I‑131 has no therapeutic effect.
Avoiding unnecessary head/neck radiation and managing iodine deficiency reduce risk; hereditary forms need genetic counseling.

exam: Explain how the Bethesda system guides management after a thyroid FNA.
